chief_complaint: excruciating electric shock pain in right cheek when brushing teeth or cold wind blows
hpi_details: 4-month history of sudden, agonizing, lightning-fast stabs of electric shock-like lancinating pain restricted strictly to the right cheek, upper lip, and right lower jaw (V2 and V3 dermatomes of the right trigeminal nerve). Each spasm lasts only 5 to 15 seconds, but occurs up to 30 times a day. Attacks are reliably triggered by trivial cutaneous stimuli: lightly touching her right cheek, brushing her teeth, chewing soft food, washing her face, or encountering a cold breeze outdoors. Between attacks, she is completely pain-free with no persistent facial ache. Has lost 4kg over 2 months because she is terrified to open her mouth or chew food.
ideas: thinks she has an infected tooth root or nerve damage in her jaw from an old dental filling
concerns: in agony and terrified to eat, drink water, or speak during flares
expectations: wants nerve-calming medication immediately and reassurance that she won't need all her teeth extracted
pmh: hypertension, osteoporosis, had two right molars extracted last month by dentist with zero relief of pain
medications: ramipril 5mg OD, alendronic acid weekly, paracetamol and ibuprofen PRN (ineffective)
social_hx: non-smoker, zero alcohol, retired school secretary, lives with husband

clinical_knowledge.topic: Classical Trigeminal Neuralgia (Tic Douloureux) evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Classical Trigeminal Neuralgia (Tic Douloureux) is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes Initiate first-line neuropathic pharmacotherapy: carbamazepine starting 100mg BID, up-titrated gradually every 3 days up to 400-800mg daily in divided doses until pain freedom achieved (or oxcarbazepine as alternative), adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: excruciating electric shock pain in right cheek when brushing teeth or cold wind blows

Key HPI features: 4-month history of sudden, agonizing, lightning-fast stabs of electric shock-like lancinating pain restricted strictly to the right cheek, upper lip, and right lower jaw (V2 and V3 dermatomes of the right trigeminal nerve). Each spasm lasts only 5 to 15 seconds, but occurs up to 30 times a day. Attacks are reliably triggered by trivial cutaneous stimuli: lightly touching her right cheek, brushing her teeth, chewing soft food, washing her face, or encountering a cold breeze outdoors. Between attacks, she is completely pain-free with no persistent facial ache. Has lost 4kg over 2 months because she is terrified to open her mouth or chew food.

Objective/Exam findings: Neurological examination: carefully inspect and test facial sensation across V1, V2, and V3 dermatomes to light touch and pinprick (CRITICAL: in classical idiopathic trigeminal neuralgia, sensory examination between attacks is completely NORMAL; any objective numbness or corneal reflex loss indicates symptomatic/secondary neuralgia from tumour or MS). Examine muscles of mastication (masseter/temporalis bulk and power). Check corneal reflex. MRI Brain with high-resolution 3D FIESTA/CISS sequences of the posterior fossa to visualize vascular loop compression (usually superior cerebellar artery compressing the trigeminal nerve root entry zone) and exclude structural causes (vestibular schwannoma, meningioma, or demyelinating plaques).
Relevant background/PMH: hypertension, osteoporosis, had two right molars extracted last month by dentist with zero relief of pain
Current medications: ramipril 5mg OD, alendronic acid weekly, paracetamol and ibuprofen PRN (ineffective)
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Classical Trigeminal Neuralgia (Tic Douloureux).
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Dental pulpitis/periapical abscess without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Bilateral pain or onset under age 40 — should prompt MRI to exclude multiple sclerosis.
management_principles: Initiate first-line neuropathic pharmacotherapy: carbamazepine starting 100mg BID, up-titrated gradually every 3 days up to 400-800mg daily in divided doses until pain freedom achieved (or oxcarbazepine as alternative)

Baseline bloods: FBC, LFTs, and U&Es (carbamazepine requires monitoring for agranulocytosis, hepatotoxicity, and syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone/hyponatraemia; check HLA-B*1502 allele in Asian patients prior to starting due to Stevens-Johnson syndrome risk)
Refer to neurosurgery for consideration of Microvascular Decompression (MVD - gold standard surgical cure) or stereotactic radiosurgery/radiofrequency rhizotomy if medically refractory
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.assessment: Classical Idiopathic Trigeminal Neuralgia (Tic Douloureux) affecting right V2 and V3 divisions secondary to neurovascular loop compression. learning_objectives: Differentiate trigeminal neuralgia from dental pathology by identifying unilateral dermatomal distribution, trigger zones, and complete inter-attack resolution
Confirm normal sensory examination and corneal reflex between attacks to rule out secondary structural trigeminal neuropathy
Prescribe first-line carbamazepine therapy while executing required safety monitoring (FBC, LFTs, sodium, and HLA-B*1502 screening)
Outline the definitive surgical option of Microvascular Decompression (MVD) for medically refractory patients

teaching.one_liner: Compression of the trigeminal nerve by a blood vessel causes brief, electric shock-like facial pain triggered by trivial touch — brushing teeth, a breeze — with completely pain-free intervals between attacks, distinguishing it from a dental problem.
differentials: Multiple sclerosis (especially if bilateral or young onset)
red_flags: Bilateral pain or onset under age 40 — should prompt MRI to exclude multiple sclerosis

must_ask.say: Does the pain feel like an electric shock, lasting just seconds?
Does light touch, like brushing your teeth or a cold breeze, set it off?
Are you completely pain-free between attacks?
Where exactly is the pain — cheek, upper lip, jaw?
Did the tooth extraction help the pain at all?

history.answer: Doctor, I have this excruciating electric shock pain shooting through my right cheek whenever I brush my teeth or feel a cold breeze.
It started out of nowhere about four months ago. At first it was an occasional zap, but it has become much more frequent over the past few weeks.
It is strictly on the right side of my face, shooting through my cheek, my upper lip, and into my lower jaw. It never crosses over to the left side.
It feels like a sudden bolt of electricity or an intense stabbing needle. It hits like lightning without any warning.
When it hits, it is a ten out of ten—pure agony that makes me freeze in place.
Each shock is very brief, lasting only about five to fifteen seconds before stopping completely.
On bad days, I can get hit by these spasms up to thirty times a day.
Yes, between the shocks, the pain disappears completely. There is no dull ache or throbbing when it stops.
Even the lightest touch sets it off, like brushing my teeth, washing my face, chewing soft food, or stepping outside into a cold wind.
Touching my right cheek or moving my mouth makes it happen. Nothing really relieves it once it fires, except waiting those few seconds for it to stop.
I have lost about four kilograms over the last two months. I am simply terrified to open my mouth or chew anything.
No, I haven't had any fever, chills, or sweats at all.
No, my face does not feel numb or weak, and my smile hasn't drooped.
No, my eyesight and hearing are completely normal, and I haven't had any double vision.
No, there has never been any rash, blisters, or sores on my face or in my mouth.
My dentist thought it might be an infection and pulled two molars on the lower right side last month, but it didn't help at all.
I tried regular paracetamol and ibuprofen, but they didn't touch the pain in the slightest.
It is ruining my life. I avoid talking, I can barely wash my face, and eating has become a terrifying chore.
I usually sleep okay because nothing touches my face in bed, but I wake up terrified of having to brush my teeth in the morning.
I was convinced it was an infected tooth root or nerve damage from an old dental filling, especially before the dentist pulled my teeth.
I am in constant terror of the next shock, and I am scared I won't be able to eat, drink water, or speak normally.
I really hope you can prescribe some medication to calm this nerve down right away, and reassure me that I don't need all my teeth pulled.
I have high blood pressure and osteoporosis. Other than that, I have been generally healthy.
I have never had any major surgeries or hospital stays, just the two tooth extractions last month.
I take ramipril five milligrams once a day for blood pressure, and alendronic acid once a week for my bones.
No, I don't have any known allergies to medicines or anything else.
No, I have never smoked in my life.
No, I do not drink any alcohol.
I am a retired school secretary, and I live comfortably at home with my husband.
My mother had high blood pressure, and my father passed away from a stroke in his eighties. No one had facial pain or neurological diseases.
I went through menopause naturally over ten years ago, so no periods or possibility of pregnancy.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 128/78 mmHg, pulse 72 beats per minute, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, temperature 36.6°C, oxygen saturation 99% on room air.
Alert, well-nourished woman sitting anxiously while shielding the right side of her face with her hand, in no acute distress at rest.
Facial skin is intact without erythema, swelling, scarring, or vesicular lesions.
Oral cavity shows healthy pink mucosa; right lower molar extraction sockets are completely healed with no signs of infection or gingival tenderness.
Temporomandibular joints demonstrate smooth symmetric opening without tenderness, clicking, or crepitus.
No tenderness on palpation or percussion over the frontal and maxillary sinuses bilaterally.
No palpable cervical, submandibular, or submental lymphadenopathy.
Bilateral corneal reflexes intact; facial muscle symmetry preserved; masseter and temporalis muscle bulk and jaw clench strength normal without deviation.
Facial sensation to light touch and pinprick is fully preserved across V1, V2, and V3 bilaterally, though light brush of the right cheek triggers a brief sharp shooting pain.
Normal muscle bulk and tone with 5/5 strength throughout all four extremities.
Finger-to-nose testing is normal bilaterally, and gait is steady with a negative Romberg sign.
